claims.claim: The impersonation design cannot deliver the namespace-escape fix T-27833 asks of it, because RFC-001 fixes the impersonated identity per Application rather than per resource: the service account is chosen once from Application.spec.destination.namespace and used for all resources in the Application. T-27833's proposal is to have the Argo CD control plane SA own kind: Namespace while an impersonated SA (stripped of namespace permissions) owns the rest, which that granularity has no way to express. The reachable path is unchanged by enabling impersonation: any user who can commit to the repository an Application syncs from writes a Namespace object whose name matches the AppProject clusterResourceWhitelist pattern (guessable, since it is group+branch derived), omits pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline, and gets privileged workloads in a namespace that the ApplicationSet's managedNamespaceMetadata was supposed to label. The only check present is the AppProject RBAC deny policy on Namespace, which governs actions through the Argo CD API/UI and does not sit at the decision point, the application controller's apply path.

The platform decision that impersonation ships behind a per-project flag and that nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed cannot hold against RFC-001's stated goal that the feature can be enabled or disabled only at the system level, applicable to all Argo CD Applications, with a single argocd-cm key (application.sync.impersonation.enabled) and a controller-wide env var and CLI flag. There is no per-project switch in the design to carry the decision. The security consequence is that an operator acting under the per-project belief who turns it on for one team silently changes the sync and diff identity for every Application in the instance, including the ones the decision meant to hold back until diff was fixed.

T-26271's confusion (CI jobs fail server-side diff as system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-server while the cluster Secret credential is deliberately broad, and the failures cluster in the projects where the sync impersonation flag was recently enabled) is explained by RFC-001's matching rule, which neither document ties to the other: with impersonation enabled, the identity is taken from the AppProject's destinationServiceAccounts entry matching the destination cluster and namespace, first valid glob match wins, falling back to the default service account of the destination namespace when nothing is configured. The reporter is chasing the cluster Secret because the standing credential is the identity they configured; the narrower identity is the one the AppProject match selected. The operational hazard is that the failure mode is a false-positive difference produced by a missing patch permission rather than by real live-state drift, and a user who proceeds to sync on that signal modifies resources on the basis of a diff computed by an identity that was never authorized to evaluate them.

RFC-001 places the impersonation seam only on the sync path (its implementation list covers GitOps Engine kubectl commands and the application controller's sync.go setting Impersonate on the SyncContext, and names no diff component), so the diff path in T-28695 keeps running as the standing cluster credential from the cluster Secret. Because Server-Side Diff issues a server-side apply dry-run and Kubernetes RBAC has no dry-run verb, authorization happens before the dry-run flag is evaluated, so every diffable resource kind forces a real patch grant onto that credential: five rounds so far, reaching Secrets, ClusterRoles/ClusterRoleBindings, CRDs, webhook configurations and ExternalSecrets. The result is a permanent, ever-widening write authority on the one credential meant to be least-privilege on external clusters, whose blast radius is every resource kind in every Application on that cluster, and whose only restraint is Argo CD's convention of always sending dryRun=All rather than any enforced boundary. Honoring destinationServiceAccounts on the diff path would put the check where the decision is made and let the least-privilege boundary on the standing credential hold.

The hydrator's repository-write Secret (argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: repository-write, holding a githubAppPrivateKey) is push authority on the branch Argo CD deploys from, and T-28239 records that the commit server pushes those commits unsigned, so if signature verification is enabled for the hydrated branch Argo CD rejects its own output. That forces operators to leave verification off on exactly the branch that feeds the cluster. Anyone who obtains that key writes manifests directly onto syncSource.targetBranch and has them applied by auto-sync with no corresponding dry commit, defeating RFC-002's premise that every change to desired state originates from a commit to the GitOps repository; the hydrator.metadata provenance file is attacker-writable in the same push, so it is not evidence. The check that would close the path is the one T-28239 proposes and does not yet exist: commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits with the public key in argocd-gpg-keys-cm and the project's SourceIntegrity policy enforcing the hydrated branch.

T-28239 scopes hydrated-commit signing to one cluster-wide signing key with per-project keys out of scope, while RFC-002 hydrates every environment into its own branch from the same commit server (environments/dev, environments/test, environments/prod in one repo). A signature under that scheme attests only that the commit server signed something, not which environment or Application it was hydrated for, so once SourceIntegrity enforcement is enabled on the hydrated branches, holding the single key produces commits accepted on the production branch just as readily as on dev. The blast radius of the one key is every environment at once, and it is also the gate on which RFC-002's push-to-stage promotion story depends, since the promoter's assurance that a staged commit is genuine reduces to that same signature.

T-27327 proposes that rollback, in both hydrator modes, write directly to the sync branch and bypass the staging branch, which turns an Argo CD UI-level permission into git push authority on the deployment branch. RFC-002's push-to-stage mode is built on the opposite assumption, that manifests land on a separate branch and an external system moves them to the deployment branch, and RFC-002's own suggested control (a naming convention such as argo/* so pushes to hydrated branches can be restricted to the argo bot) does not stop this, because the rollback commit is pushed by that same bot credential. The result is a path from the Argo CD rollback control to arbitrary prior manifest state on the deployed branch that never passes the promotion gate; T-27327 also notes there are no additional controls on the specific revision of the branch, and leaves blocking subsequent commits out of scope, so a rolled-back state can be silently rolled forward again by the next hydration.

The PRD's Security Considerations dismiss the deletion-order feature on the ground that no additional roles or privileges are needed to delete deployed applications in a specific order, which is true of the privilege required and false of the blast radius it creates. T-28511 shows the deletionOrder the PRD introduces converting one ordinary action, deleting a single child Application in the UI, into a self-sustaining condition: with the Reverse order the controller waits for one Application to be fully deleted before moving to the next, a child stuck Progressing means that wait never completes, and the wave restarts from the top in a delete/recreate loop across the whole ApplicationSet. The stuck resource is attacker-supplied in the reproduction (a crashlooping app committed to a path the git generator scans), so the same repository write access that T-27833 treats as low trust is enough to arm it. No check sits at the controller: the mitigation on record is a runbook step telling operators to switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce before any manual delete, and T-27846 establishes that the progressive-sync metrics that would show a wave restarting, or which Applications a sync is waiting on, do not exist yet, so nothing records that this is happening.
